new_statements.quote: As in many of the languages of the Eastern New Guinea Highlands Stock, tone in Usarufa is closely linked with stress. In some of the Highland languages tone sequences are conditioned by stress while in others stress is conditioned by tone sequences. The latter is true in Usarufa. The three phonemic tones, high, falling, and low, condition stress as follows: stress occurs on the first high-tone syllable of a sequence of all high-tone syllables or of such a sequence following low-tone syllables; on the last high- or falling-tone syllable preceding low tone; and on the last low-tone syllable in a sequence of all low tones.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Usarufa with an empty rule and no existing statements; this source supplies the rule: tone language (H, F, L), stress sub-phonemic and tone-conditioned, one stress per phonological phrase, placed on the first H of an H-run, the last H/F before L, or the final syllable of an all-L phrase. Nothing in the catalog is contradicted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Usarufa has three contrastive tones (high, falling, low). Stress is not contrastive ('stress being subphonemic will be unmarked', p. 191) and is fully predictable from the tone pattern of the phonological phrase / stress group, which carries exactly one stress ('a unit having one stress, whose placement is determined by the nucleus of falling and/or high tones', p. 191). Placement: (a) in an all-high run, or a high run after lows, on the FIRST high syllable; (b) where a high or falling syllable is followed by low, on the LAST high/falling syllable before the low; (c) in an all-low sequence, on the LAST (final) low syllable. Examples pp. 192-193: ["máámím:á] 'a type of tree' (initial), [ma"yáímá] 'work' (second), [ilá"qóne] 'It is good' (third), [a"nêma] 'a type of bird' (on the falling syllable), [ku'kabu"wo] 'Scrape it!' (final, all-low stem). Domain is the phrase, not the word: one stress per phonological phrase, and each stress group contains at most one series of high/falling syllables (Bee 1973 features p. 215).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. The phonological phrase / stress group has a single (primary) stress: 'Stress group: a phonological unit with one primary stress whose placement is determened by the distribution of pitch features within the unit' (Bee 1973, features, p. 205). The only case of more than one stress is intonational (fn. 2, p. 194, see exceptions).
new_statements.exceptions: Fn. 2, p. 194: 'Questions, emphatic predicated nouns, and proper name calling forms have a falling tone on the word final suffix with corresponding stress. This use of the falling tone is interpreted as intonation because it is fixed.. and because it creates a new tone pattern of more than one series of high tones, and, therefore, more than one stress.' Bee 1973 (features) pp. 214-215: 'Stress may be considered a component of the pitch feature being conditioned by tone placement. Each stress group contains no more than one series of syllables with high and/or falling pitch.' with fn. 5 deferring to ch. XII; pp. 216-217 (scan page 7) note a non-contrastive lengthening of a high-pitch penultimate vowel or of a low penult before a high final. Bird's own page adds tonal remarks only ('all Usarufa words must have at least one high tone'; 'High tone is lowered after low'; scant evidence for the high vs falling contrast).
new_statements.identity_note: Bee & Glasgow's material was gathered in the village of Mairapaga, Orono district, about thirty miles south and west of Kainantu (p. 190, fn. 1), monolingually. Bird's 2011 recordings are of two speakers, Ima'o Ta'asata (one of Bee's original informants) and Waks Mark. Bee notes that Usarufa and Auyana are so closely related that they may be dialects of one language (features, p. 205; grammar, pp. 224-226 argue for separate-language status). No sub-dialect of Usarufa is distinguished in the stress statement.

tone_statements.citation: Bee, Darlene and Glasgow, Kathleen Barker (1962). Usarufa tone and segmental phonemes, Studies in New Guinea Linguistics, OLM 6:111-27. Also in The languages of the Eastern Family of the East New Guinea Highland Stock, ed. by Howard McKaughan, pp. 190 203.
tone_statements.quote: Prosodic features designated in the orthography are lengthened nasals (written nn or mm) and contrastive pitch. Usarufa is a tone language with three tones. High pitch (synonymous with stress) is indicated by an acute accent (´ ); high-falling pitch is indicated by a circumflex (ˆ); and low pitch is unmarked (Bee and Glasgow 1973:191).
tone_statements.summary: Three tones, following Bee and Glasgow: high (acute), high-falling (circumflex), low (unmarked). Word stress is derived from tone: a falling or lone high syllable takes primary stress.

sources.quote: p. 229: phoneme classes are defined by position in the 'stress group'; 'Tone is distinctive with high, low, and falling contrasts. For greater detail of both tone and segmental phonemes see Chapters XII and XIII.' p. 230: every nominal stem belongs to one of two tone classes and every verb stem to one of three tone classes, which determine tone sandhi. p. 234: '(There is one and only one nucleus of high tones within a single word and/or descriptive phrase.)' No independent word-stress rule is stated.
